provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Electricity: current
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state Ohm's law and explain its application in circuits.
The students should be able to solve problems involving current voltage and resistance.
The students should be able to differentiate between series and parallel circuits.
Introduction:
We have previously studied charges and electric fields. Today we will build on this knowledge to understand how electric current flows through circuits.
Content:
Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points and inversely proportional to the resistance between them. This is expressed as I = V/R where I is current in amperes V is voltage in volts and R is resistance in ohms. In a series circuit the current remains constant throughout while voltage divides across components. In a parallel circuit the voltage remains constant while current divides. For example when charging a phone with a power bank the current flows through the circuit to charge the battery.
Class activity:
Students will construct simple series and parallel circuits using batteries bulbs and connecting wires and measure current and voltage at different points using multimeters.
Evaluation questions:
1. State Ohm's law.
2. Calculate the current flowing through a resistor of 10 ohms connected to a 12V battery.
3. Differentiate between series and parallel circuits.
4. Why do homes use parallel circuits for lighting?
Summary:
Ohm's law is fundamental to understanding electric circuits and differentiating between series and parallel configurations helps in designing electrical systems.

topics.title: Electricity: fields
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the concept of electric fields.
The students should be able to calculate capacitance for different capacitors.
The students should be able to compare primary and secondary cells.
Introduction:
Having studied electric current we now turn to electric fields and energy storage devices like capacitors and cells.
Content:
An electric field is a region of space around a charged particle where a force would be exerted on other charged particles. The strength of an electric field is measured in volts per meter. A capacitor stores electrical energy in an electric field between two conductive plates separated by an insulator. Its capacitance is given by C = Q/V where Q is charge and V is voltage. Primary cells like dry cells cannot be recharged while secondary cells like lead-acid batteries can be recharged. For example the battery in a danfo bus is a secondary cell that can be recharged.
Class activity:
Students will measure the capacitance of different capacitors using a capacitance meter and observe how connecting capacitors in series and parallel affects the total capacitance.
Evaluation questions:
1. What is an electric field?
2. Calculate the capacitance of a capacitor that stores 0.01C of charge when connected to a 10V supply.
3. Differentiate between primary and secondary cells.
4. Why are parallel capacitors used in power supply circuits?
Summary:
Electric fields form the basis of understanding how capacitors and cells store electrical energy for various applications.

topics.title: Magnetism
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe magnetic fields around different types of magnets.
The students should be able to calculate magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor.
The students should be able to explain the earth's magnetic field.
Introduction:
We have studied electric fields and now we will explore magnetic fields and forces which are closely related to electricity.
Content:
Magnetic fields are regions where magnetic forces can be detected represented by field lines going from north to south pole. The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor is given by F = BILsinθ where B is magnetic field strength I is current L is length of conductor and θ is the angle between conductor and field. The Earth has a magnetic field that protects us from solar radiation and helps compasses work. For example the magnetic field of a bar magnet can be visualized using iron filings.
Class activity:
Students will plot magnetic field patterns around bar magnets and electromagnets using compass needles and iron filings.
Evaluation questions:
1. Describe the magnetic field around a bar magnet.
2. Calculate the force on a 2m wire carrying 3A of current in a 0.5T magnetic field if the wire is perpendicular to the field.
3. How does the Earth's magnetic field protect us?
4. What is the difference between a permanent magnet and an electromagnet?
Summary:
Magnetic fields are invisible forces that can be visualized and have practical applications in motors and generators.

topics.title: Electromagnetic induction
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
The students should be able to describe how generators work.
The students should be able to differentiate between step-up and step-down transformers.
Introduction:
After studying magnetism we will now explore how changing magnetic fields can produce electricity through electromagnetic induction.
Content:
Faraday's law states that the induced electromotive force in a closed circuit is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux through the circuit. Generators convert mechanical energy to electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field. Transformers change voltage levels using electromagnetic induction with alternating current. A step-up transformer increases voltage while a step-down decreases it. For example the NEPA transformer in your neighborhood steps down voltage for home use.
Class activity:
Students will assemble a simple generator using a coil magnets and a galvanometer to observe induced current when the coil rotates.
Evaluation questions:
1. State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
2. How does a generator produce electricity?
3. Differentiate between step-up and step-down transformers.
4. Why is AC voltage preferred for long distance transmission?
Summary:
Electromagnetic induction is the principle behind generators and transformers which are essential for electricity distribution.

topics.title: Heat: temperature and measurement
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define temperature and heat.
The students should be able to explain the construction and use of thermometers.
The students should be able to convert between different temperature scales.
Introduction:
We have studied electricity and now we turn to heat energy which is another important form of energy in our daily lives.
Content:
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance while heat is energy transferred due to temperature difference. Thermometers measure temperature using the expansion of liquids like mercury or alcohol. The three main temperature scales are Celsius Fahrenheit and Kelvin. To convert Celsius to Kelvin add 273. For example during the harmattan season temperatures can drop significantly requiring warmer clothing.
Class activity:
Students will calibrate simple thermometers using ice water and steam points and measure temperatures of different substances.
Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between temperature and heat.
2. Explain how a liquid-in-glass thermometer works.
3. Convert 25°C to Kelvin and Fahrenheit.
4. Why is mercury used in thermometers despite its toxicity?
Summary:
Temperature measurement is essential in science and daily life with various scales used depending on the application.

topics.title: Heat: transfer
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain conduction convection and radiation.
The students should be able to give examples of each mode of heat transfer.
The students should be able to explain factors affecting heat transfer.
Introduction:
Having studied temperature measurement we now explore how heat energy moves from one place to another through different mechanisms.
Content:
Conduction is heat transfer through direct contact between particles without movement of the material itself. Convection involves heat transfer through the movement of fluids due to density differences. Radiation is heat transfer through electromagnetic waves without a medium. Metals conduct heat well while gases are poor conductors. For example a metal spoon in hot soup conducts heat to your hand while a kerosene stove heats a room through convection and radiation.
Class activity:
Students will demonstrate conduction by touching different materials convection by observing colored water in a beaker and radiation using two cans one painted black and one silver in sunlight.
Evaluation questions:
1. Explain conduction with an example.
2. How does convection occur in fluids?
3. Why are thermos flasks silvered?
4. Which mode of heat transfer does not require a medium?
Summary:
Heat occurs through three mechanisms each with different applications in our daily lives and technology.

topics.title: Heat: gas laws
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state Boyle's law and Charles' law.
The students should be able to solve problems using gas laws.
The students should be able to explain the ideal gas law.
Introduction:
We have studied heat transfer and now we will explore how gases behave under different temperature and pressure conditions.
Content:
Boyle's law states that at constant temperature the volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure (P1V1 = P2V2). Charles' law states that at constant pressure the volume of a given mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (V1/T1 = V2/T2). The ideal gas law combines these as PV = nRT where P is pressure V is volume n is number of moles R is gas constant and T is temperature. For example when you inflate a bicycle tire the pressure increases as volume decreases.
Class activity:
Students will verify Boyle's law using a syringe and pressure gauge and Charles' law using a gas bulb and thermometer in water baths of different temperatures.
Evaluation questions:
1. State Boyle's law.
2. A gas occupies 2L at 1 atm pressure. What will its volume be at 3 atm pressure if temperature is constant?
3. State Charles' law.
4. Explain why a balloon expands when heated.
Summary:
Gas laws describe the relationships between pressure volume and temperature of gases with applications in many technologies.

topics.title: Modern physics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the photoelectric effect.
The students should be able to differentiate between nuclear fission and fusion.
The students should be able to explain applications of modern physics.
Introduction:
After studying classical physics we now explore modern developments in physics including quantum mechanics and nuclear physics.
Content:
The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a material when light shines on it explained by Einstein using photons. Nuclear fission is splitting heavy nuclei into lighter ones releasing energy used in power plants. Nuclear fusion is combining light nuclei to form heavier ones releasing more energy than fission. Modern physics applications include solar panels nuclear power and medical imaging. For example solar panels on roofs convert sunlight to electricity using the photoelectric effect.
Class activity:
Students will research and present on applications of modern physics in medicine energy production and communication.
Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the photoelectric effect.
2. Differentiate between nuclear fission and fusion.
3. Give one application of modern physics in medicine.
4. Why is fusion not yet commercially viable for power generation?
Summary:
Modern physics has revolutionized our understanding of matter and energy with applications in technology and medicine.

topics.title: Mock paper one
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to apply physics concepts to solve examination problems.
The students should be able to manage time effectively during examinations.
The students should be able to identify areas of weakness in their knowledge.
Introduction:
Today we will simulate the WAEC Physics Paper 1 examination to help you prepare for the actual exam.
Content:
The mock paper will cover all topics from the term including electricity magnetism heat and modern physics. Questions will include multiple choice theory and calculation problems similar to WAEC standard. Time management is crucial as you have 1 hour to complete 50 questions. Practice reading questions carefully eliminating wrong options and using dimensional analysis for calculations. For example when solving a circuit problem first identify known values then apply appropriate formulas.
Class activity:
Students will write the full mock paper under examination conditions. After completion we will mark the paper and review difficult questions together.
Evaluation questions:
The mock paper itself serves as evaluation with questions covering all topics taught this term.
Summary:
The mock examination provides valuable practice for the WAEC exam helping students identify areas needing further study.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall and apply key physics concepts.
The students should be able to solve past WAEC questions effectively.
The students should be able to improve their examination techniques.
Introduction:
As we approach the final exams we will focus on revision and practicing past WAEC questions to build confidence and improve performance.
Content:
We will review key concepts from the term including electricity magnetism heat and modern physics. Past WAEC questions will be used to demonstrate examination techniques and common pitfalls. Pay attention to question wording units in calculations and showing all working steps. For example in a calculation problem always write down the formula substitute values and show units in your answer.
Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past WAEC questions and present their solutions to the class for discussion and feedback.
Evaluation questions:
Past WAEC questions will be used for evaluation covering all topics with emphasis on areas where students showed weakness in the mock exam.
Summary:
Regular practice with past questions is essential for exam success and building confidence in physics problem-solving.
